methods.label: Find the mixed pairs first
methods.sourceMethod: Count the blue students outside blue-blue pairs, identify their yellow partners, and pair the remaining yellow students.

annotationRationale: Relate student counts to pair counts using two students per same-color pair and one of each color per mixed pair. Comparing the color totals provides a second route.

classificationReview.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is suitable for counting the three types of pairs. No repair is needed.

review.questionCheck: The blue-blue pairs use 46 blue students, leaving 11 mixed pairs and 64 yellow students in yellow-yellow pairs. Therefore there are 32 yellow-yellow pairs, choice B. The counts, choices, recorded answer, and supplied shared-question evidence agree.
review.alternativeMethodCheck: The mixed-pair count and the color-total difference argument are useful distinct approaches, and both are supplied. No further route is needed.
review.annotationCheck: cnm_p111 appropriately assesses relationships between group totals and pair counts. cnm_p112 is reasonable arithmetic support, but these solutions do not independently assess parentheses or operation-order proficiency.
review.areaCheck: Counting & Probability is suitable for counting the three types of pairs. No repair is needed.

methodReviews.mathCheck: The successive counts are \(2\cdot23=46\), \(57-46=11\), and \((75-11)/2=32\). Every blue student outside a blue-blue pair has exactly one yellow partner, so no students or pairs are omitted or counted twice.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: The method matches the written LIVE and AoPS counting route. It correctly uses source-informed-original attribution and supplies its own explanation. The shared AMC 12 question contributes no separate written method.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The first move is motivated, and the explanation consistently distinguishes numbers of students from numbers of pairs. Each subtraction and division has an explicit counting meaning.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: cnm_p111 fits the total-versus-parts relationships and the conversion between pairs and students. No unsupported immediate node is present.

nativeLayerJudgments.CN: The exact native cnm_p111 link applies through additive totals and fixed group size, although its price and distance examples are not exercised.
nativeLayerJudgments.US: The supplied rate links offer at most limited overlap through two students per pair. Fractional unit rates in 7.RP.A.1 are not used; none of these links establishes full-standard coverage.
nativeLayerJudgments.ailleo: cnm_p111 is appropriate for the quantitative relationships actually explained; arithmetic remains supporting knowledge.

methodReviews.mathCheck: Mixed pairs contribute equally to both color totals. Consequently \(2(YY-BB)=75-57=18\), giving nine more yellow-yellow pairs and hence \(YY=23+9=32\). The cancellation and factor of two are both justified.
methodReviews.sourceMethodCheck: The written references use the mixed-pair counting route rather than this difference argument. Labeling this method original with no claimed source references is consistent with the supplied evidence.
methodReviews.pedagogyCheck: The explanation makes clear why setting aside mixed pairs preserves the difference and why the remaining student difference must be divided by two. It independently determines the answer.
methodReviews.directNodeCheck: cnm_p111 applies to comparing additive totals and converting a difference of student counts into a difference of pair counts. No more precise replacement is supplied in the packet.

nativeLayerJudgments.CN: The exact native quantitative-relationships link reasonably covers the additive comparison and fixed group size used here.
nativeLayerJudgments.US: The accepted unit-rate links are peripheral to this difference argument. Neither fractional rates nor explicit unit-rate modeling is assessed.
nativeLayerJudgments.ailleo: cnm_p111 supports the stated total-and-group relationships. The explanation itself supplies the cancellation argument without invoking an unsupported concept.
